The reported 96% is misleading:

Consider that ~8.5% of adults in the US have been diagnosed with cancer, and assume that number's close to the number who actually have it.

Assume 300,000,000 people in the US, 75% of which are adults (225,000,000). These nice round numbers are fairly close to the 2014 census results.

Then, about 19,000,000 of those adults will have cancer at some point.

Following the link from the article, we can find the actual paper and they (thankfully) publish all four the the key success rates of the test in Figure 1G in the paper (direct link?). 97% is the success rate among people who have cancer; it's 94% accurate among people who don't.

For a given adult in the US receiving the 97% accurate test (that's 94% accurate if they don't have cancer), the possible outcomes are:

Actually Has Cancer Actually Is Healthy Test's Totals
Test Says Cancer 97% = 18,430,000 6% = 12,360,000 30,790,000 (14%)
Test Says Healthy 3% = 570,000 94% = 193,640,000 194,210,000 (86%)
Actual Totals 8.5% = 19,000,000 91.5% = 206,000,000 225,000,000

As you can see, in the US adult population, the test will report that 30,790,000 individuals have cancer, when only 18,430,000 of those 30m actually do, meaning that "If the test says you have cancer, there is a 59.8% chance you actually do" - which is the number that most patients probably care about.

On the flip side, though, if the test says you don't have cancer... 194,210,000 individuals would get that result, and of them 570,000 (0.3%) would have cancer - meaning if the test says you don't have cancer there's a 99.7% chance that you actually don't. That is useful.

In its current form, this test is far more useful for ruling out cancer than diagnosing its presence. But the 96% is still relevant - it means the process fundamentally works, and since they appear to have trained a genetic algorithm (ha!), there's hope that it can reach a level of accuracy that would allow it to be an effective positive diagnostic tool.

In any case, thank you for sharing.

The realities of tuition free education
There are degrees we absolutely should subsidize like medical doctors, provided the student can pass the tests necessary to prove his ability to study and work in the field.

I disagree. It would probably just end up dramtically raising the cost of that degree, which would mean the government has to pay for more, higher taxes and everyone is worse off. Even the people paying for the degree would save money in the long term without the subsidies

Generally libertarians desire as little government intervention as possible. At most, it should be localized rather than a large central planning bureaucracy. Subsidizing education goes against this, especially favoring one or a handful of degrees over others. For one, it sends mixed signals in that it might cause potential students to gravitate towards the degree that is cheaper for them. However, with the flood of new medical graduates, you could potentially see overall salaries in the medical industry go down as the hospitals, etc. may be able to select applicants from a larger pool and the new students will have to take a cut to make themselves more likely to get a job. Or we can look at the education aspect and realize that as government has involved itself in education loans, or subsidized college, tuition has only gone up. Which hurts everyone. More taxes to pay for the higher cost, and costs go up because "hey, someone is still willing to pay this!"...it feeds itself and everyone is the poorer for it. The point is, this is how a libertarian would look at it--at the "unforseen" costs, and whether anyone should be favored over others. History shows how inefficient, counter-productive and even dangerous a government can be. So government intervention should not be encouraged.
